revision.revised_memo: Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968), holds that police may stop and frisk on reasonable suspicion that a person is armed and involved in crime. This authority may support our position, but the analysis of how its standard applies to our facts, and of any contrary arguments, is still to be done. The court may or may not reach the same conclusion.
changes: Removed "AMAZING news!!!" and the repeated exclamation marks: shouting and emotional language are not allowed in a neutral memo (rule 4).

Replaced "this is a slam dunk for us" with a statement that the authority may support our position and that application to the facts and contrary arguments remain to be analyzed: removes overconfidence and one-sided framing.
Replaced "the court will absolutely agree" with "the court may or may not reach the same conclusion": removes certainty language about the outcome.

Restated the Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968) holding to match the firm's one-line holding (stop and frisk on reasonable suspicion that a person is armed and involved in crime); the original said only "allows stops on reasonable suspicion". Name, citation and year unchanged and verified.
No fabricated cases were present and no other cases were added or removed; no [AUTHORITY NEEDED] or [CITE-CHECK NEEDED] markers were required.
